fields:
Someone sings while the wheat is cut.

Not a performance. It is the rhythm of the work: one line drawn out long, then the sound of the sickle going through, then the next line. Whoever it is stands at the far end, and you cannot make out the words.

A few of the others come in now and then. Not together.

There are birds on the cut ground. A dozen or so, walking about between the stubble, taking up the grain that fell.

They are not afraid of people. You go along the edge and they move two steps aside, no more.

When the frost goes in the morning the whole field steams white.

It is not fog. It comes up out of the ground. The moment the sun is out it starts to go, and it goes fast; you watch it finish inside a quarter of an hour.
forest:
You find a row of mushrooms along a fallen trunk.

A dozen of them, graded by size, all on one line: the side that was facing up when the tree went down.

You do not pick them. You look a while and walk on.

There is a deer a long way off among the trees.

It stands, turns its head, watches you for some seconds. You do not move either.

Then it goes. Not at a run. It walks. It does not consider you worth running from.

When the wind comes down off the slope the sound of the whole wood travels from high to low.

The crowns first, then the middle, and only then the dead leaves at your feet.

One gust takes three or four seconds to get through.
stable:
The chestnut rests its head on your shoulder.

It does this to everyone who comes in. Gregor says it was how it asked for food when it was young; after a while nobody gave it any, but the gesture stayed.

Its breath is heavy, and hot.

You go into the stable at night and all eight are there.

Not one of them awake, but you can hear them breathing. Eight different rhythms, drifting slowly out of one another and slowly back.

You stand in the doorway a while before you go.
kitchen:
Martha is teaching a tenant’s girl to cut.

The child is twelve or thirteen and holds the knife wrong. Martha does not correct her. She only slows her own hands to a third of their speed and lets the girl watch.

Half an hour of cutting later the girl has fixed it herself.

The kitchen window has begun to hold its condensation well before winter.

Somebody has drawn on it. A crooked house, a horse. Low down, at a child’s height.

When Martha wipes the windows she goes around that part.
forge_chapel:
Somebody is asleep inside when you come in.

A tenant, sitting against the wall, his head fallen onto his shoulder. He came in on his way past to get warm, most likely, and then went off.

The light of the hearth is on his face.

You back out and pull the door to, quietly.
default:
The maple leaves come down like snow.

Not one at a time. A gust arrives and lays another layer. The flagstones are covered soon enough that there is no stone to see, and it makes a sound to walk on.

You stop in the middle of the avenue and look back.

Nobody is watching you.

Elena is airing the quilts in the yard.

A quilt that has been out in the sun has a smell to it. You could not say what the smell is, but you know you knew it as a child.

She beats each one three times.

When there is no wind at dusk the chimney smoke goes straight up.

It gets a long way up before the wind that lives up there takes it and leans it east.

You stand in the courtyard and watch. There is nothing else left in the day to do.
market:
Somebody is playing at the edge of the square.

An old man on a low stool, the instrument across his knees. Not a fiddle: one of the local kind, with a very flat body.

There is no hat in front of him and no bowl. He is not asking for money. He is playing.

A few of the people going past stop and listen a while, then go.
